title: New & Expectant Mothers at Work
blurb: Why pregnancy and new motherhood change workplace risks, and how we support colleagues with sensible adjustments.
siteNotes: Where a colleague can rest or express milk in private, and how to ask for it
Which manager carries out the specific risk assessment in each department
legalNotes: Employers must assess risks to new and expectant mothers and act on them: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, regs. 16 to 18. Not re-checked in this conversion; the trainer states the duty only in general terms.

cards.title: New & Expectant Mothers at Work
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why some risks matter more in pregnancy and after birth
- say what a pregnant colleague or new mother should do
- support a colleague without making assumptions

cards.title: A legal duty
cards.body:
When a colleague is pregnant, has recently given birth or is breastfeeding, some risks that are normally minor can become more significant.

We have a legal duty to protect them.

> Looking after new and expectant mothers is the law, and it is also the decent thing to do.

left.title: It does mean
items: We look closer at the risks

cards.title: What deserves a closer look
cards.body: During pregnancy and after birth, take a closer look at:

items.title: Standing
items.text: Very long periods on your feet

items.title: Shifts
items.text: Long or night shifts and fatigue

items.title: Food safety
items.text: Some foods carry infections that are riskier in pregnancy

cards.title: Tell your manager
cards.body:
The key step is communication. If you are pregnant or a new mother, tell your manager as early as you feel comfortable.

That lets us do a risk assessment for your situation.

items.title: Tell
items.text: Your manager, as early as you are comfortable

items.title: Assess
items.text: A specific risk assessment for you

items.title: Agree
items.text: You and your manager agree duties

cards.title: What reasonable adjustments might be
cards.body: Adjustments depend on the person. They might include:

cards.title: Be supportive, never assume
cards.body:
For everyone else the message is simple: be supportive and understanding.

Never make assumptions about what a colleague can or cannot do. That is for them and their manager to agree.

Managers must act promptly when told.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- We have a legal duty to protect new and expectant mothers
- Tell your manager early so a risk assessment can be done
- Pregnancy does not mean a colleague cannot work: we adjust sensibly
- Be supportive and never assume; the person and their manager agree duties
- Managers act promptly once told

cards.q: We have a legal duty to protect new and expectant mothers at work.
cards.why: Some normally minor risks become more significant in pregnancy and after birth, and we have a legal duty to protect colleagues.

cards.q: What is the key step a pregnant colleague or new mother should take?
options: Tell their manager early so a risk assessment can be done
Wait until after the baby is born before saying anything
Ask a friendly colleague to cover duties quietly for them
Change their own duties without telling anyone
cards.why: Communication is the key step. Early notice lets the manager do a specific risk assessment and make adjustments.

cards.q: Which of these is a risk that deserves a closer look during pregnancy?
options: Answering the phone at reception
Heavy lifting, long standing, night shifts
Greeting guests as they arrive
Using the staff noticeboard daily
cards.why: Heavy or awkward handling, standing for long periods, certain chemicals, long or night shifts and some food-safety risks all need a closer look.

cards.q: Being pregnant means a colleague cannot do any work at all.
cards.why: None of this means someone cannot work. It means we adjust things sensibly.

cards.q: After being told, a manager should:
options: Wait a few months to see how things go
Carry out a specific risk assessment and make adjustments
Do nothing until a doctor writes to the venue
Move the colleague to a quieter shift without asking
cards.why: Managers must act promptly: a risk assessment for the colleague's situation, then any reasonable adjustments.

cards.q: Reasonable adjustments might include lighter duties, more breaks or a private space to rest.
cards.why: Lighter duties, more breaks, changes to hours or somewhere private to rest or express milk are all examples.

cards.q: What is the simple message for colleagues about supporting a new or expectant mother?
options: Offer to take over any task you think is too hard
Be supportive, and do not assume what they can or cannot do
Ask them regularly whether they should still be working
Tell the guests so they can be extra patient
cards.why: Be supportive and understanding. What a colleague can or cannot do is for them and their manager to agree.

cards.q: Some foods carry infections that are riskier during pregnancy.
cards.why: Food-safety risks are one of the hazards to look at more closely in pregnancy.

cards.q: Who agrees what duties are suitable for an expectant mother?
options: Any colleague on shift
The guests she is serving
The person and their manager
Her closest friend at work
cards.why: It is for the colleague and their manager to agree, never for others to assume.

cards.q: Managers should act promptly once told about a pregnancy.
cards.why: Managers must act promptly when told so the risk assessment and adjustments are not delayed.
